# Ordinary differential equations {#sec-ordinary-differential-equations}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 1, Session 3. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

@sec-foundations solved the SIR model to establish the theory; this
chapter is about the *tools*. We work through the `OrdinaryDiffEq` workflow in
depth: defining an `ODEProblem`, choosing the `Tsit5` solver, evaluating the
dense continuous solution with interpolation, and — most importantly — using
**callbacks** to inject events such as a time-limited lockdown and to detect the
epidemic peak automatically. These techniques recur in every dynamical chapter
that follows.

## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- assemble an `ODEProblem` from a kernel, initial condition, timespan, and
  parameters;
- solve it with `Tsit5` and say what `reltol`/`abstol` control and when to
  tighten them;
- evaluate the dense interpolant `sol(t)` at arbitrary times, and say how that
  differs from indexing the stored solution as `sol[i, :]`;
- apply a `PresetTimeCallback` to change a parameter mid-simulation (a
  lockdown);
- use a `ContinuousCallback` to detect an event (the infectious peak) exactly.

## Model assumptions and classification

The base model is the deterministic SIR system of @eq-ch01-sir, unchanged. For
the intervention example we make the transmission parameter time-dependent:
during a lockdown window $[t_1, t_2]$ the per-contact transmission probability
$\beta$ drops to a reduced value $\beta_\text{lock}$, then returns. The model
remains deterministic and continuous; the only new ingredient is a piecewise-
constant parameter.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Deterministic |
| Time | Continuous |
| State | Continuous |
| Parameters | Piecewise-constant (lockdown example) |

## Equations

The governing equations are those of @sec-foundations, written here with an
explicit time-dependent force of infection:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda(t) S, \quad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda(t) S - \gamma I, \quad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \gamma I, \quad
\lambda(t) = \frac{\beta(t)\, c\, I}{N}.
$$ {#eq-ch03-sir}

The lockdown makes $\beta$ a step function of time:

$$
\beta(t) =
\begin{cases}
\beta_\text{lock}, & t_1 \le t < t_2,\\
\beta, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ch03-lockdown}

The infectious peak is the instant at which growth turns to decline,
characterised by

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda(t) S - \gamma I = 0,
$$ {#eq-ch03-peak}

which a `ContinuousCallback` can locate to solver tolerance by root-finding on
this expression.

## Julia implementation

### Problem, solver, and interpolation

An `ODEProblem` bundles the kernel, initial state `u0`, timespan `tspan`, and
parameters `p`. `Tsit5` is a 5th-order adaptive Runge–Kutta method suitable for
non-stiff problems like SIR.

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-solve
using OrdinaryDiffEq

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N      # eq-ch03-sir
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
tspan = (0.0, 80.0)

prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p)
sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
length(sol.t)     # number of adaptive steps chosen by the solver
```

`reltol` and `abstol` are the accuracy request: the solver shrinks its step until
the estimated local error falls below `abstol + reltol * |u|`. The defaults are
`reltol = 1e-3`, `abstol = 1e-6`, which is ample for plotting a trajectory —
@sec-foundations used them. We tighten both to `1e-8` here because this chapter
locates an event by root-finding and then checks that event time against a
brute-force scan; the callback can only be as accurate as the trajectory it runs
on. Tightening tolerances costs solver steps, so ask for the accuracy the
question needs rather than the smallest number available.

Note also that no `saveat` appears here. Without it the solver stores exactly the
steps its adaptive controller chose — hence `length(sol.t)` above, which is not a
round number. That is fine, because `Tsit5` produces a *dense* output: `sol(t)`
returns a high-order interpolant at any time inside the span, whether or not that
point was stored.

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-interp
grid = 0.0:1.0:80.0
I_on_grid = [sol(t)[2] for t in grid]     # interpolated infectious counts
(sol(12.5)[2], I_on_grid[13])
```

This is the deliberate change of idiom from @sec-foundations. There, `sol[2, :]`
gave the infectious compartment at the *stored* times; here `sol(t)` evaluates it
at times we choose. Use `sol[i, :]` when the solver's own grid is what you want,
and `sol(t)` whenever the grid is yours — a regular observation grid, a finer
grid for plotting, or a single instant. The interpolant is what makes a
continuous-time model comparable with daily surveillance data later on.

### A lockdown via `PresetTimeCallback`

A `PresetTimeCallback` fires an `affect!` function at prescribed times. The
`affect!` receives the *integrator* — the solver's live state — and changes
something about the run in flight. Here it replaces the parameters to enact
@eq-ch03-lockdown: $\beta$ drops to $0.025$ at day 10 and returns at day 30.

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-lockdown
using DiffEqCallbacks

t1, t2 = 10.0, 30.0
β_base, β_lock = 0.05, 0.025

start_lockdown!(integrator) = (integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = β_lock,)))
end_lockdown!(integrator)   = (integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = β_base,)))

cb = CallbackSet(PresetTimeCallback([t1], start_lockdown!),
                 PresetTimeCallback([t2], end_lockdown!))

prob_lock = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p)
sol_lock = solve(prob_lock, Tsit5(); callback = cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
(maximum(sol[2, :]), maximum(sol_lock[2, :]))   # peak I: baseline vs lockdown
```

`merge` returns a new `NamedTuple` with `β` replaced and every other field
carried over, which we assign back to `integrator.p`. The parameters therefore
stay the same named container used everywhere else in the course — there is no
need to switch to a mutable vector and index it positionally. `CallbackSet`
combines callbacks; the solver applies each at its own times.

### Peak detection via `ContinuousCallback`

`ContinuousCallback` root-finds a scalar condition and fires when it crosses
zero. Setting the condition to $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$ (@eq-ch03-peak) locates
the infectious peak exactly, without scanning saved points.

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-peak
peak_times = Float64[]
peak_values = Float64[]

function dIdt(u, p)                          # eq-ch03-peak
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    return λ * S - p.γ * I
end

peak_cb = ContinuousCallback(
    (u, t, integrator) -> dIdt(u, integrator.p),          # condition: root of dI/dt
    integrator -> (push!(peak_times, integrator.t);       # affect!: record the event
                   push!(peak_values, integrator.u[2])))

solve(prob, Tsit5(); callback = peak_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
(peak_times, peak_values)
```

The two functions handed to `ContinuousCallback` have different signatures, and
this trips people up. The **condition** is given `(u, t, integrator)`, so the
state arrives directly as `u` and we write `u[2]`. The **affect!** is given only
the integrator, so the same state is reached as `integrator.u[2]`. Reading `u`
inside an `affect!`, or `integrator.u` inside a condition, is the usual first
error.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch03-lockdown
#| fig-cap: "Infectious curve without intervention (solid red) and with a lockdown reducing β by half over days 10–30 (dashed blue, shaded window). The vertical line marks the callback-detected baseline peak. The lockdown flattens and delays the peak."
using CairoMakie

tt = 0.0:0.25:80.0
I_base = [sol(t)[2] for t in tt]
I_lock = [sol_lock(t)[2] for t in tt]

fig = Figure(size = (720, 440))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
          title = "SIR with a lockdown intervention")
vspan!(ax, t1, t2; color = (:grey, 0.15))
lines!(ax, tt, I_base; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "no intervention")
lines!(ax, tt, I_lock; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, linestyle = :dash,
       label = "lockdown (days 10–30)")
vlines!(ax, peak_times; color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "detected peak")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

## Validation

**Conservation.** The adaptive solution must conserve the population at every
step (@eq-ch01-conservation):

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-check-conservation
all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), sol.u)
```

**Interpolation consistency.** The dense interpolant evaluated at a saved time
must reproduce the stored state, confirming `sol(t)` is faithful:

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-check-interp
t_check = sol.t[10]
isapprox(sol(t_check), sol.u[10]; atol = 1e-8)
```

**Peak detection.** The callback-detected peak must coincide with the maximum of
a densely sampled solution and satisfy $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t \approx 0$:

```{julia}
#| label: ch03-check-peak
dense_t = 0.0:0.01:80.0
dense_I = [sol(t)[2] for t in dense_t]
brute_peak_time = dense_t[argmax(dense_I)]
residual = dIdt(sol(peak_times[1]), p)
(isapprox(peak_times[1], brute_peak_time; atol = 0.05), isapprox(residual, 0.0; atol = 1e-4))
```

All three checks return `true`: the solver conserves population, its interpolant
is self-consistent, and the event-detected peak matches the brute-force maximum
while zeroing the growth rate.

## Interpretation and limitations

The `OrdinaryDiffEq` workflow separates *what* the model is (the kernel and
problem) from *how* it is solved (the algorithm and tolerances) and *what
happens during* the solve (callbacks). This separation scales: the same
`ODEProblem` can be handed to a stiff solver, differentiated for sensitivity
analysis, or fitted to data with no change to the kernel. Callbacks turn a plain
integrator into an event-driven simulator — lockdowns, vaccination pulses, and
threshold-triggered interventions all follow the same pattern. The limitations
are those of the deterministic SIR model itself (@sec-foundations): no
stochasticity, homogeneous mixing, exponential infectious periods. The lockdown
here is a deterministic, perfectly-timed switch; realistic interventions involve
uncertainty and feedback, taken up in the interventions and control chapter. For
the full API see the
[OrdinaryDiffEq documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/OrdinaryDiffEq/stable/) and
the
[event-handling and callback guide](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqDocs/stable/features/callback_functions/).

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch03-ex1}

Extend the lockdown study by sweeping the intervention strength: for
$\beta_\text{lock} \in \{0.045, 0.035, 0.025, 0.015\}$ over the same window
10–30, solve the model and record the peak infectious count and its timing using
the `ContinuousCallback`. Describe how intervention strength trades off peak
height against peak timing.

### Exercise 2 {#ch03-ex2}

Add a fourth state $C$ for cumulative incidence with
$\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}t = \lambda(t) S$, solve the baseline model, and use the
dense interpolant `sol(t)` to compute daily incidence as the difference
$C(t) - C(t-1)$ on the integer-day grid. Verify that summing the daily
increments recovers the final cumulative incidence $C(80)$.
